title: New Scientist Book Club reads Dark Eden by Chris Beckett
content: The New Scientist Book Club is reading Dark Eden by Chris Beckett We went out by a path that led through a big clump of flickering starflowers and then into Batwing. A whole bunch of Batwing grownups and newhairs were in their clearing banging away at a giant redlantern tree with their blackglass axes, working in the pink light of its flowers. We walked round the edge of their clearing to Family Fence, dragged away the branches at the opening, and went out into open forest. No more shelters and campfires ahead of us now: nothing but shining trees. Hmmmph, hmmmph, hmmmph, went the trees. Hmmmmmm, went forest. We walked for a waking under the light of the treelanterns, slashing down whatever birds and bats and fruit we could get as we went along, and finally stopped to rest at the big lump of rock called Lava Blob. Old Roger handed us out a gritty little seedcake each, made of ground-up starflower seeds, so we could have something in our bellies, and then we settled down with our backs against the rock, so we didn’t have to worry about leopards sneaking up behind us. There were lots of yellowlantern trees round there, which we didn’t get so much back in Family, and also yellow animals called hoppers that came bouncing out of forest on their back legs and wrung their four hands together while they looked at us with their big flat eyes and went Peep peep peep. But hoppers were no good to eat and their skins were no use either, so we just chucked stones at them to make them go away and let us sleep in peace. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When we woke up, Starry Swirl was still bright bright in sky. We ate a bit of dry cake and off we went again, under redlanterns and whitelanterns and spiketrees, with flutterbyes darting and glittering all round us and bats chasing the flutterbyes and trees going hmmph, hmmph, hmmph like always, until it all blurred together into that hmmmmmmmmm that was the background of our lives. After a few miles we came to a small pool full of shiny wavyweed and all us newhairs took off our wraps and dived into the warm water for crabfish and oysters to eat. All the boys watched Tina Spiketree diving in, and they all thought how graceful she was with her long legs, and how smooth her skin was, and how much they wanted to slip with her. But when she came up she swam straight to me, and gave me a dying oyster with the bright pink light still shining out of it. “You know what they say about oysters, don’t you, John?” she said. Tom’s neck, she was pretty pretty, the prettiest in whole of Family. And she knew it well well. In another couple of hours we reached the place where Peckham Hills began to rise up out of forest of Circle Valley, and started to climb up through them by Monkey Path, which isn’t really a path, but just a way we know through the trees. The trees carried on up the slopes – redlanterns and whitelanterns and scalding hot spiketrees – and there were flickering starflowers growing beneath them, just like in the rest of forest. Streams ran through them down from darkness and ice, heading towards Greatpool, still cold cold but already bright and glittering with life. And small creatures called monkeys jumped from tree to tree. They had little thin bodies, and six long arms with a hand on the end of each. Handsome Fox shot one with an arrow, and was pleased pleased with himself, even though they were all bones and sinews and only give a mouthful of meat, because they move fast and are hard to aim at with those big blotches on their skin that flash on and off as they swing among the lanternflowers. As we climbed up it got colder. The starflowers disappeared, the trees became smaller, and there weren’t any monkeys any more, only the occasional smallbuck darting away through the trees. And then the trees stopped and we came out from the top edge of forest onto bare ground. Pretty soon, when we’d climbed above the height of those last few little trees, we could see whole of Circle Valley spread out below us – whole of Eden that we knew, with thousands and thousands of lanterns shining all the way from where we stood on Peckham Hills to Dark shadow of Blue Mountains away in the distance, and from Rockies over the left, with the red glow of Mount Snellins smouldering in middle, to the deep darkness over to our right that was Alps. And above all of it the huge spiral of Starry Swirl was still shining down. Of course, with no trees to give off light with their lanternflowers or to warm the air with their trunks, it was dark dark up there – you could only just barely make things out in the starlight and the light from the edge of forest – and it was cold cold, specially on our feet. But us newhairs dared each other to run up as far as the snow. The ice felt like it was burning, it was so cold, and most kids took ten twenty steps, yelled and came running down again. But I took Gerry right up to the ridge of the hill and then, ignoring Old Roger yelling at us to come back, went far enough down the other side so that the others couldn’t see us. “We’ve made our point now, haven’t we, John?” Gerry said, shivering. We only had waistwraps on, and buckskins round our shoulders, and our feet were hurting like they’d been skinned. “Shall we go back down to rest of them now?” Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time My cousin Gerry was about a wombtime younger than me – his dad was giving his mum a slip, in other words, about the time that I was born – and he was devoted to me, he thought I was wonderful, he’d do just about anything I asked. “No, wait a minute. Wait a minute. Be quiet and listen.” “Listen to what?” “To the silence, you idiot.” There was no hmmmmmmmm of forest, no hmmph, hmmph, hmmph of pumping trees, no starbirds going hoom, hoom, hoom in the distance, no flutterbyes flapping and flicking, no whoosh of diving bats. There was no sound at all except a quiet little tinkle of water all around us coming out from under the snow in hundreds of little streams. And it was dark dark. No tree-light up there. The only light came from Starry Swirl. We could barely make out each other’s faces. It made me think about that place called Earth where Tommy and Angela first came from, way back in the beginning with the Three Companions, and where one waking we would all return, if only we stayed in the right place and were good good good. There were no lanterntrees back there on Earth, no glittery flutterbyes or shiny flowers, but they had a big big light that we don’t have at all. It came from a giant star. And it was so bright that it would burn out your eyes if you stared at it. “When people talk about Earth,” I said to Gerry, “they always talk about that huge bright star, don’t they, and all the lovely light it must have given? But Earth turned round and round, didn’t it, and half the time it wasn’t facing the star at all but was dark dark, without lanterns or anything, only the light the Earth people made for themselves.” “What are you talking about, John?” Gerry said, with his teeth chattering. “And why can’t we go back down again if you just want to talk?” “I was thinking about that darkness. They called it Night, didn’t they? I’m just thinking that it must have been like this. What you get up here on Snowy Dark: it’s what they would have called Night.” © Chris Beckett This is an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett (Corvus), the November read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here. When you make a purchase via the links on this page, we receive a commission.
summary: The New Scientist Book Club is reading Dark Eden by Chris Beckett. The excerpt describes a journey through a forest with starflowers, redlantern trees, and creatures such as hoppers and monkeys.
author: New Scientist

title: Scientists find fruit and vegetable skins contain more fibre than flesh
content: Fruit and vegetable skin is often rich in fibre Ekaterina Vasileva-Bagler/Getty Images Some people are convinced that fruit and vegetable skin are particularly nutritious, and now scientists have confirmed the idea. They have discovered that these parts of fruits and vegetables often contain far more fibre than the flesh we normally consume. The finding suggests cooks are unwittingly discarding fibre-rich food by chucking out the seeds, skins and stems of fruits and vegetables when preparing a meal. Home cooks and caterers should adopt “root to tip” eating and start cooking with squash peel, watermelon rind and pepper stalks to improve the public’s intake of dietary fibre, the team says. Advertisement Our food system is vulnerable to El Niño, warns UK climate minister “We’ve really got to shift our purchasing habits to buy whole fruits and vegetables, and then use all of the fruits and vegetables in dishes,” says Rachel Gibson at King’s College London. Gibson and her colleagues tested the fibre content of 12 fruits and vegetables, including butternut squash, kiwi fruit, watermelon, broccoli and bell pepper. The team measured the fibre content both in the parts typically consumed and the parts that usually go to waste. They found that, in 10 of the 12 produce types, the normally wasted components contain more fibre than the commonly consumed parts. Butternut squash seeds and skin, for example, contained 9.25 grams of fibre per 100 grams, compared with 2 g of fibre per 100 g of squash flesh. Meanwhile, the skin and core of a pineapple core contains 450 per cent more fibre than the flesh. These skin and core components are often tough to chew, but the researchers say they can be blended, grated or roasted to make them more palatable. Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter Just 4 per cent of British adults meet the recommended minimum daily intake of 30 g of dietary fibre, with the average adult consuming around half that per day. Gibson suggests caterers could use the findings to design fibre-rich meals using more produce that would otherwise go to waste. This could reduce food waste and cut costs for commercial kitchens, as well as increasing dietary fibre intake, she says. King’s College London’s canteen piloted a “root to tip” menu in May 2025. Meals included a West African peanut stew made with all of a butternut squash, kale stalks and leek tops, and a watermelon salad featuring pickled watermelon rind. Simple menu tweak can nudge people into choosing climate-friendly food Rejigging the meal choices on offer in a canteen can prompt people to make healthier, climate-friendlier decisions Eating a larger proportion of harvested fruit and vegetables will also improve the resilience of the food system in the face of climate shocks, says Gibson. “Everything we pull out of the ground that we can eat, we should be eating.” Christian Reynolds at City St George’s University of London says the research is an “exciting investigation”. But he points out that the most carbon-intensive food waste is meat and dairy products. Reducing fruit and vegetable waste is therefore “part of the solution, but it’s not the only thing we need to do”, he says. Journal Reference: International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition DOI: 10.1080/09637486.2026.2734852
summary: Researchers from King’s College London measured fibre in 12 produce items and found that in 10 of them the skins, seeds or cores contain more fibre than the flesh. The study suggests adopting a “root to tip” approach could boost dietary fibre intake and reduce food waste.
author: New Scientist

title: Binance Hit by Biggest Crypto Heist, $6.36B Stolen in 20 Minutes
content: Binance is the biggest cryptocurrency exchange ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Binance has been hit with the biggest ever cryptocurrency heist, in which billions of dollars of reserves were drained in just 20 minutes. From 8:05pm on 29 October, $6.36 billion in cryptocurrencies were shifted from wallets in a coordinated attack believed to have originated from a North Korean-linked hacking unit called TraderTraitor. This group was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit crypto exchange in February 2025. The US Treasury has previously said that such stolen funds are used to finance North Korea’s nuclear missile programme. Advertisement Despite cryptocurrency’s founding idea of decentralisation, meaning no one has singular control over the money flowing through the network, there are some large single points of failure. It is thought one of these was the cause of the Binance hack, which gave access to a system the exchange uses to authorise transfers out of customers’ accounts. Quantum computer quickly mines cryptocurrency while using less energy In a statement, Binance said its early investigations indicate the security incident may stem from a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. TRM Labs, a cybersecurity firm, suggests that preparations for the attack may have begun several days ago. The company claims it has found no evidence that the private cryptographic keys used to authorise transactions were stolen. Instead, the attackers appear to have gained access to the software that requests withdrawals, potentially allowing them to instruct Binance’s own systems to approve the transfers. However, the investigation is continuing and the firm has said in a subsequent statement there may have been “additional points of breach”. “It shouldn’t be possible for a single [developer] PC to be compromised and somehow for that to allow the entire exchange to be compromised,” says Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK. “I don’t understand how that can happen unless they’ve got the most ridiculous operational security.” If that is the case, it highlights how precarious major financial hubs in the crypto world can be to single points of failure. Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter “You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened,” says Clive Summerfield at FARx, a cybersecurity company. “Most crypto platforms are as centralised as any bank, with a small number of privileged individuals controlling billions. The difference is that once crypto is transferred, it’s gone.” That centralisation can be a blessing as well as a curse, though: cryptocurrencies Tether and Circle have been able to freeze billions of dollars of stolen coins, stymying the hackers in attempts to transfer about half the stolen funds any further. Woodward says the Binance incident potentially strikes a distinction between crypto security and more traditional finance. “You would hope there’d be things like two-man rules [where two separate people have to approve a change] or things that banks have for changing critical systems, but it doesn’t look like those were in place.”
summary: Binance Hit by Biggest Crypto Heist, $6.36B Stolen in 20 Minutes.

title: Birmingham physicists create miniature universe, observe time emerging without a clock
content:
Scientists created a miniature universe in the laboratory, a setup that could help answer one of physics' biggest mysteries: what is time and where it comes from.  

Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch.  

The experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.
summary: Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. The experiment showed that time could emerge from changes inside the system without relying on an external clock.

content: Astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope have made a discovery that challenges the leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense hydrogen fog roughly 13 billion years ago. title: Voyager 1 to Reach One Light‑Day from Sun on Nov 18 2026
content:
November’s Night Sky Notes: Light‑Day Away

In 1977 NASA launched two identical spacecraft, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, to take advantage of a planetary alignment that occurs once every 175 years. The alignment of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune allowed the twin probes to use six gravity assists to visit each of the four largest planets in the outer solar system. The mission delivered close‑up images and scientific data on the gas and ice giants, including several of their moons.

After completing their encounters with Saturn in the early 1980s, the Voyager probes went their separate ways. Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune, while Voyager 1 captured a final portrait of the solar system—excluding Mercury and Mars—including the last image of Earth, the pale blue dot. The Voyager missions set the stage for later orbiter missions such as Galileo to Jupiter and Cassini to Saturn.

Each spacecraft carries a 12‑inch phonograph record known as the Golden Record. The record contains spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 musical tracks, 116 images, and other sounds from Earth. The outer cover is etched with the Sun’s position relative to 14 pulsars and includes instructions for playback. The record itself is plated with copper and gold, while the cover is made of aluminum and electroplated with an ultra‑pure sample of the isotope uranium‑238, which has a half‑life of 4.468 billion years.

Both Voyager probes crossed the heliopause—the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind meets the interstellar medium—in August 2012 (Voyager 1) and November 2018 (Voyager 2). NASA’s Deep Space Network continues to communicate with the spacecraft and track their positions. At the time of this article, the Canberra antenna was tracking Voyager 1 at a distance of 25.80 billion km, or just over 16 billion miles, from Earth.

On November 18, 2026, 49 years after launch, Voyager 1 will reach the one‑light‑day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. This milestone highlights the vast distances measured in light‑time units, a concept familiar from science‑fiction and stargazing alike. The Voyager spacecraft remain outside the heliosphere, the protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well beyond Pluto’s orbit.
summary: 2 min read November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away NASA’s Voyager mission took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. The twin spacecraft revealed details about Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune – using each planet’s gravity to send them on to the next destination.

title: GLP-1 weight‑loss drugs may worsen rising eating disorder rates
content:
A new report published in JAMA Psychiatry indicates that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa increased by 71% between 1990 and 2023. By 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people were living with one of these two disorders, a figure researchers expect to rise to 21.8 million by 2050. The study, led by Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, utilized statistical models to analyze data from 204 countries and territories. The researchers calculated that these conditions cost the world the equivalent of approximately 3.83 million years of healthy life in 2023, measured in disability-adjusted life years.

Clinical experts suggest that environmental factors, including social media and the COVID-19 pandemic, have contributed to this rise. Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, notes that social media comparisons, influencers, and diet trends serve as precipitating events for eating disorders. Research from the University of Melbourne found that TikTok algorithms delivered 4,343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” to users with these conditions compared to those without. Additionally, data from 2021 showed that hospitalizations for eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020, a trend experts link to the social isolation of lockdowns.

Cheri Levinson, a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville, reports seeing more patients with severe symptoms than at any point in her 20-year career. She states that many of these patients are misusing GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which she describes as a potential trigger for worsening conditions. In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs, with 10% appearing to misuse them. Levinson believes this misuse rate is an underestimate and reports cases of children developing eating disorders after being prescribed these medications for medical reasons or purchasing them online.

The accessibility of GLP-1s has increased, with a Gallup survey indicating that 15% of Americans have used these drugs for weight loss. Drug companies are developing new formulations, and versions are available through compound pharmacies or online sources. Bulik expresses concern that GLP-1s may lead to faster and more extreme weight loss in individuals with anorexia nervosa, resulting in patients arriving at treatment in advanced stages of illness that are difficult to reverse. Both Levinson and Bulik are continuing to study the impact of these drugs on eating disorders.

In response to these concerns, Bulik contributed to research and clinical guidelines published earlier this month. These guidelines recommend that doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing GLP-1s, provide more patient education, and implement robust monitoring for individuals taking the drugs. Levinson adds that she is not surprised if the number of eating disorder cases doubles again, noting that she is currently seeing patients as young as eight and nine years old with the conditions. The true impact of eating disorders is likely higher than reported figures, as anorexia and bulimia represent less than half of all eating disorders, according to Levinson.
summary: A JAMA Psychiatry study reported a 71% increase in the incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa from 1990 to 2023, with an estimated 18.1 million people affected in 2023. Clinical psychologists say that GLP‑1 weight‑loss drugs are being misused by people with eating disorders, potentially worsening symptoms and contributing to earlier onset.

title: iOS app Oh My Hours tracks wasted Instagram and TikTok time in hour blocks
content: The iOS app Oh My Hours brutally shames users by tracking how many hours they’ve lost to scrolling. It divides each day into hour‑long blocks and highlights the blocks spent on Instagram and TikTok, offering a new approach to curbing screen time.
summary: The iOS app Oh My Hours takes a new approach to curbing screen time. It splits the day into hour‑long blocks and shows which blocks were wasted on Instagram and TikTok.

title: TraderTraitor linked to $6.3 B Binance hack executed in 20 minutes
content: A $6.3 billion hack of Binance was reportedly executed in just 20 minutes. Multiple crypto‑tracing firms have identified the North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor as a possible perpetrator of what they describe as the largest digital heist in history, with billions of cryptocurrency likely unrecoverable.
summary: Multiple crypto‑tracing firms say the North Korean hacker group TraderTraitor may be behind the $6.3 billion Binance hack. The breach reportedly took only 20 minutes and is described as the largest digital heist in history, with billions of crypto likely gone for good.
author: Wired

title: Wikimedia Foundation warns bad AI copyright ruling could harm open web
content:
The Wikimedia Foundation filed an amicus brief on Friday in a group of landmark lawsuits that pit publishers, including The New York Times, against OpenAI and Microsoft. In the brief, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia argues that courts should legally protect large‑language models that train on copyrighted material while exempting chatbots that merely regurgitate that material to users.  

Wikimedia warns that a strictly black‑and‑white ruling could either strip Wikipedians of useful AI‑based tools or threaten the open web. The foundation takes no side in the litigation but expresses concern that the parties’ positions push for an overbroad approach.
summary: Wikimedia Foundation warns bad AI copyright ruling could harm open web.

content: Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, was midway through defending her record during the final debate of the midterms when an audience member cut her short. "I'm terrified," a man shouted. "AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our water." Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. But the fear echoing through the auditorium wasn't so easily dismissed. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine's most volatile campaign issues. Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Le …
summary: During the final midterm debate, Republican Sen. Susan Collins was interrupted by a protester who warned that AI data centers are destroying the climate and poisoning water. Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the protester to her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson as the data center issue becomes a volatile campaign topic.
author: The Verge

title: Binance Reports $6.3 Billion Crypto Theft, Claims to Cover Losses
content:
Binance announced that $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency has been stolen from its platform, a theft that is believed to be the largest hack in the history of digital assets. The exchange has stated that the loss is the result of a coordinated cyberattack and that the incident represents a record‑breaking breach.

In a series of updates posted to X, Binance confirmed that user funds remain safe and that roughly $3 billion of the impacted assets have already been frozen. The company has pledged to cover any losses incurred by users as a result of the hack.

Binance also disclosed that it has an emergency reserve fund of about $1.3 billion, based on its last valuation, to protect user assets in such situations. Additionally, the company has set aside more than $6.34 billion of its own funds to cover the incident, with $5 billion of those funds earmarked for this purpose.
summary: Binance says it will cover all loses resulting from the hack. | Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Turbosquid Binance has disclosed that $6.3 billion worth of crypto funds have been stolen from the platform, in what's believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency hack on record.
author: The Verge

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (what a name) has one of the nicest screens I've seen on a laptop. The current Mini LED MacBook Pros are great, but the OLED has those even inkier blacks. Apple calls it a "reference-caliber display," which is a very Apple-y marketing term, but it walks the walk by being the first laptop display with support for Apple CMF 2026 color …

title: Apple HomeView and Amazon Echo Show 16 poised as family computers
content: Three years ago, I wrote an obituary for the smart display. The category - smart speakers with touchscreens attached - was stuck with a few underpowered gadgets from Google and Amazon that tried to do too much and did too little well. Back then, I also laid out what they needed to do to improve. This month, Apple and Amazon launched new smart displays that check nearly every box on that list. Based on my brief hands-on time with Apple's first smart display, the $299 HomeView, and Amazon's $499.99 Echo Show 16, a ground-up rebuild of its smart display line, these could finally turn the smart display into what it should have been all along: …

After brief hands‑on testing of Apple’s $299 HomeView and Amazon’s $499.99 Echo Show 16, the author says they could finally fulfill the smart‑display role as a family computer.

title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says AI math output will continue despite mathematicians' concerns
content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the company’s recent flood of AI‑generated mathematical results and expressed sympathy for researchers who are trying to keep up. In a Thursday episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast, he said, “I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works,” while adding, “But I do have empathy for the method.”  

Altman made clear that OpenAI will not pause its output and hinted that more discoveries may follow from the company’s growing stockpile. His remarks are among the first public statements in which the OpenAI chief directly addressed the impact of the firm’s work on the mathematics community.
summary: Sam Altman, OpenAI CEO, said he sympathizes with mathematicians overwhelmed by the company's AI-generated results. He told the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday that OpenAI will not stop the math onslaught and may release more discoveries.
author: The Verge

title: Anthropic files 335-page S-1 prospectus, urging investors to believe in transformative AI
content: Investing in any stock is kind of like gambling in the sense that you're betting your money on a company's future performance. But how do you bet on a technology that could, in the worst-case scenario, "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," or best case, "bring forth an age of miracles"? To some extent, Anthropic suggests in a letter at the top of its S-1 filing, you have to just believe. Anthropic's 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, is part of a steady hype escalation in Silicon Valley's interactions with Wall Street. In some ways, it's not even that bizarre; SpaceX IPO'd in June after filing an S-1 that referenced din …
summary: Anthropic's 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, contains a letter telling investors they must simply believe in the technology. The filing reflects a hype escalation in Silicon Valley's ties to Wall Street, exemplified by SpaceX's June IPO after its own S-1 filing.
author: The Verge

title: Cowboy Space reveals specifications for its Big Iron medium‑lift rocket
content: Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It's been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that's what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I'm a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn't have much hardware to show at this week's big reveal. In other words, don't mistake style for substance. But we're rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck. As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Virgin's new rocket plane reaches home port. The first of Virgin Galactic's new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports. Virgin Galactic expects the craft's first commercial spaceflight to take place "early" in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS Unity, in 2024. Read full article Comments
summary: Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It's been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that's what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins.

title: Film “You Can See Everything” portrays Elizabeth Holmes’ final days before prison
content:
In 2015, Elizabeth Holmes was celebrated as Silicon Valley’s youngest and richest self‑made female billionaire, with her company Theranos valued at $9 billion. The company’s reputation collapsed after accusations of fraud regarding its blood‑testing device, leading to a high‑profile trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison.

The former entrepreneur has returned to the headlines with the film You Can See Everything, which portrays the final days before Holmes entered prison after exhausting her appeals. The movie is co‑directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim and has been described as a surreal, absurdist piece that has generated widespread enthusiasm and hype, with some calling it the best film of the year.

Critics, however, have offered counter‑views. The reviewer notes that while the film contains entertaining moments—particularly in its second half—it delivers little new insight into Holmes or the Theranos saga. The film is described as shallow, running in circles, and not justifying the intense hype surrounding it.
summary: The documentary, co‑directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, depicts the period just before Elizabeth Holmes began her 11‑year sentence after being convicted on four fraud counts. The reviewer calls the film shallow and lacking fresh insight despite its hype.
author: Ars Technica

title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid launches with 1.5‑L series e‑Power system
content:
Nissan supplied a flight from Washington, DC, to Santa Barbara, California, and lodging so that Ars could test‑drive the company’s new 2027 Rogue Hybrid. The outlet notes that it does not accept paid editorial content.

The 2027 model is the latest iteration of Nissan’s best‑selling Rogue SUV and is being introduced with the newest version of the brand’s e‑Power hybrid system, which Ars evaluated in February. Unlike most current hybrids that operate as parallel systems—using an internal‑combustion engine and an electric motor together to drive the wheels—Nissan’s e‑Power uses a series‑hybrid layout. In this configuration the gasoline engine functions solely as a generator to charge the traction battery, while the electric motor provides propulsion.

Under the hood, the Rogue Hybrid is equipped with a 1.5‑liter, three‑cylinder turbocharged direct‑injection engine that produces 148 hp (110 kW). The engine is limited to 5,200 rpm and is tuned primarily to charge the battery rather than to handle direct drivetrain loads. This design enables a reported thermal efficiency of 42 percent, a figure the article compares only to Formula 1 power units.

Visually, the vehicle features a crisp shut line and slim horizontal headlights that the writer likens to a Range Rover aesthetic. These details, combined with the series‑hybrid powertrain, define the 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid as a model that aims to deliver electric‑vehicle‑like driving dynamics without requiring external charging.
summary: Nissan introduced the 2027 Rogue Hybrid, the latest version of its best‑selling Rogue SUV equipped with the e‑Power series‑hybrid system. It is powered by a 1.5‑liter three‑cylinder turbocharged engine that produces 148 hp (110 kW), revs to 5,200 rpm to charge the traction battery, and achieves roughly 42 % thermal efficiency.
author: Ars Technica

content: Runware is constructing a factory designed to produce prefabricated AI data centers on an assembly line. The company’s next challenge will be demonstrating that it can deliver these facilities at the required scale.

title: Voice actor stars in Black Tides Draga’s Wake after 50 years of gaming
content:
Greg Strangis initiated a creative partnership 16 months ago by inviting the author to his garage to review his game, Black Tides Draga’s Wake. Strangis introduced himself by telling the author, “I listen to you on the radio and I keep hearing your voice in my head!” This request led to the author voicing the main character in the title.

The experience of performing the role involved making noises the author had not produced since their honeymoon. It also resulted in a favorite moment as a father, marking a unique milestone for the individual who has been playing video games for 50 years.
summary: He is voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake, a role that has made him make noises he hasn’t made since his honeymoon and created a favorite moment as a father. Greg Strangis introduced himself 16 months ago and invited him to his garage to look at the game.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Meta staff discussed a ‘whisper strategy’ to discredit critic Jonathan Haidt, court papers show
content:
Court documents show Meta employees discussed a “whisper strategy” aimed at undermining Jonathan Haidt, a U.S. social psychologist whose book The Anxious Generation influenced debates on online safety. The internal memos indicate staff considered ways to get the academic community to disavow Haidt and to discredit him publicly.

The documents also note that Haidt’s work helped shift discussion toward stricter measures, including Australia’s under‑16 ban on certain social‑media features. Meta’s planning centered on countering his influence.
summary: Court documents reveal Meta employees considered a “whisper strategy” to get the academic community to disavow Jonathan Haidt. The staff sought to discredit Haidt, a social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation, whose book helped tip the debate toward stricter online safety measures such as Australia’s under‑16 ban.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Workers face unsafe conditions and fear retaliation at European datacentres
content:
Investigations by the Guardian and Investigate Europe have highlighted that workers constructing the growing number of datacentres across Europe face hazardous conditions and fear retaliation for speaking out. The reporting points to instances of unsafe practices and concerns about exploitation among the workforce.

One example involves a 34‑year‑old electrical tester named Sandu at a Google datacentre in Saint‑Ghislain, Belgium. In March, after nearly ten hours on duty, he received a call for a last‑minute assignment that required testing the safety and integrity of electrical wiring. Sandu said such late‑night jobs were routine and that refusing could lead to dismissal. Although a protective suit was stored nearby, retrieving it would have added about fifteen minutes, and with people waiting he chose to proceed without it.
summary: Workers face unsafe conditions and fear retaliation at European datacentres.
author: Guardian Technology

title: North Korean group blamed for $6.3bn Binance hack, biggest crypto theft
content: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack? Business live – latest updates The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by an industry-record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit. Binance has scrambled to freeze the affected assets, with about $3bn located so far. The company gave no update on the other $3.3bn as Binance’s co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.
summary: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, was hit by an industry‑record $6.3bn hack, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit. Binance has frozen the affected assets, has located about $3bn so far, and co‑founder Yi He said the company will cover all hacking losses.
author: Guardian Technology

content: Flowers were placed at Patrick Stewart’s Hollywood Walk of Fame star after reports of the British actor’s death at age 86. In Los Angeles, visitors gathered around the star to remember Stewart’s celebrated screen roles.

content:
Nine orangutans rescued from devastating wildfires in Indonesian Borneo have returned to the forest after weeks of rehabilitation.  
Among the rescued group are four mothers with their young, and three of those females are expecting another baby.
summary: Nine orangutans rescued from devastating wildfires in Indonesian Borneo have been released back into the forest after weeks of rehabilitation. The group includes four mothers with their young, and three of the females are expecting another baby.

content: China has denied allegations that a spy plot was aimed at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s spokesperson told AFP on Friday that the company’s regional cloud customers receive only ordinary business information, not sensitive trade secrets, and that no data relevant to national security is shared.

title: TotalEnergies posts record quarterly profit while keeping fuel prices below rivals
content:
Hundreds of thousands of French citizens are expected to protest the high cost of living again this weekend. The demonstrations come amid a backdrop of rising consumer concerns over everyday expenses.

Oil and gas giant TotalEnergies has reported record profits for the quarter ending September. The company has maintained fuel prices lower than those of its rivals at its pumps, yet motorists are questioning whether the firm could reduce prices further.
summary: TotalEnergies reported record profits for the quarter to September. It has kept fuel prices at its pumps lower than rivals, even as hundreds of thousands in France are expected to protest the high cost of living.
author: France 24

title: Tanzania marks one year since violent 2025 election that left many traumatised
content: Tanzania is marking the first anniversary of the bloody 2025 election that has left many people traumatised. The vote held on October 29, 2025 saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan win with 98 percent of the vote after most opposition candidates were excluded. The result triggered days of protests that security forces brutally suppressed. Many government critics continue to fear abduction, arbitrary arrest and politically motivated prosecutions.
summary: Tanzania is marking the first anniversary of the October 29, 2025 election that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan declared winner with 98 percent of the vote after most opposition candidates were excluded. Critics say they continue to fear abduction, arbitrary arrest and politically motivated prosecutions following the security forces’ brutal suppression of days of protests.
author: France 24
